cards.back: Flat, non-palpable change in skin colour < 1 cm.
Flat, non-palpable change in skin colour > 1 cm.
Raised, palpable solid lesion < 1 cm.
Raised, flat-topped lesion > 1 cm, often formed by papules joining.
Solid, raised lesion > 1 cm that extends deeper into the dermis.
Small fluid-filled blister < 1 cm.
Fluid-filled blister > 1 cm.
Small raised lesion filled with pus.
Transient, itchy, oedematous papule or plaque, as in urticaria.

Linear erosion caused by scratching.

cards.front: Atopic eczema: typical sites in infants vs adults
cards.back: Infants: face and extensor surfaces. Older children and adults: flexures (elbows, knees).
Atopic eczema, asthma and allergic rhinitis (hay fever).
Regular emollients, plus topical corticosteroids for flares.
Widespread herpes simplex infection on eczema: punched-out erosions and fever. An emergency.
Loss-of-function mutation in a skin barrier protein; a major risk factor for atopic eczema.
Irritant contact dermatitis (direct damage, e.g. detergents) and allergic contact dermatitis (type IV hypersensitivity, e.g. nickel).
Used to identify the allergen in allergic contact dermatitis.
Greasy yellow scale on the scalp, eyebrows and nasolabial folds; linked to Malassezia yeast.
Itchy vesicles on the palms and soles; a type of hand eczema.
Coin-shaped, itchy eczema plaques, often on the limbs.
Well-demarcated red plaques with silvery-white scale on extensor surfaces (elbows, knees) and the scalp.
New psoriasis lesions appear at sites of skin trauma.
Pitting, onycholysis, oil-drop discolouration, subungual hyperkeratosis.
Many small teardrop-shaped psoriasis plaques, often 2–4 weeks after a streptococcal throat infection.
Inflammatory arthritis in people with psoriasis; can cause dactylitis and DIP joint involvement.
Pinpoint bleeding when psoriasis scale is scraped off.
Psoriasis covering most of the body; risk of fluid loss and infection. An emergency.
Sterile pustules on red skin, either localised (palms/soles) or generalised.
Stress, infection, trauma, alcohol, smoking, some drugs (lithium, beta-blockers).
Increased sebum, follicular hyperkeratinisation, Cutibacterium acnes colonisation, inflammation.
Open (blackheads) and closed (whiteheads) blocked pilosebaceous follicles; non-inflammatory acne lesions.
Topical retinoid or benzoyl peroxide, or both.
Oral retinoid for severe nodulocystic acne; highly teratogenic, needs pregnancy prevention.
Facial flushing, persistent central facial redness, telangiectasia, papules and pustules; no comedones.
Thickened, bulbous nose from sebaceous overgrowth in advanced rosacea.
Ice-pick, boxcar, rolling and hypertrophic scars.
Asymmetry, Border irregularity, Colour variation, Diameter > 6 mm, Evolving.
Depth of melanoma invasion in mm; the most important prognostic factor.
Superficial spreading, nodular, lentigo maligna, acral lentiginous.
Pearly papule with rolled edges and telangiectasia; may ulcerate (rodent ulcer).
Very rarely; it is locally invasive.
Keratotic, scaly nodule that may ulcerate, on sun-exposed skin.
Actinic keratosis. The in situ form is Bowen's disease.
Rough, scaly patches on sun-damaged skin; premalignant.
Staged excision with margin checks; used for basal cell carcinoma on the face.
UV exposure, sunburn, fair skin, immunosuppression, family history, many naevi.
A mole that looks different from the patient's other moles; suspicious for melanoma.
Handheld magnified examination of pigmented lesions to help diagnose melanoma.
Superficial bacterial skin infection with honey-coloured crusts; Staph aureus or Strep pyogenes.
Infection of the dermis and subcutaneous tissue: spreading redness, warmth, swelling.
Fungal infection: annular scaly plaque with central clearing (ringworm).
Fungal infection of the feet (athlete's foot), between the toes.
Skin scrapings for microscopy and culture; Wood's lamp for some.
Intensely itchy rash with burrows in the finger webs, from the Sarcoptes scabiei mite.
Pearly umbilicated papules caused by a poxvirus; common in children.
Painful vesicular rash in a dermatome from reactivation of varicella zoster virus.
Malassezia fungal infection causing hypo- or hyperpigmented scaly patches on the trunk.
Superficial form of cellulitis with a sharply raised border; usually streptococcal.
Itchy wheals that each last < 24 hours; from mast cell histamine release.
Deeper swelling of the dermis and subcutaneous tissue, often the lips and eyelids.
Tense blisters in older adults; autoantibodies against hemidesmosomes.
Flaccid blisters and mouth erosions; autoantibodies against desmoglein; Nikolsky sign positive.
Skin shears off with gentle lateral pressure; seen in pemphigus vulgaris and SJS/TEN.
Severe drug reaction with mucosal involvement and skin detachment < 10% of body surface area.
Itchy vesicles on the elbows, knees and buttocks; associated with coeliac disease.
Target lesions, often after herpes simplex infection.
